chapters.name: Chapter 1: The CDA path and keeping children safe

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What the CDA is and the steps to earn it
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the steps to earn the CDA in your setting.
This lesson builds toward: Using the Council for Professional Recognition's page for your setting, you will list the education, experience, portfolio, exam and Verification Visit steps for the CDA, with the hours and time windows correct.
The Child Development Associate (CDA) Credential is granted by the Council for Professional Recognition. It shows you can put the CDA Competency Standards into practice with young children. There are pathways for Preschool, Infant-Toddler, Family Child Care and Home Visitor settings, and each has its own requirements page.
For the Preschool setting (children 3 to 5 in a center), the Council's page lists: a high school diploma or GED (or enrollment as a junior or senior in a high school early childhood career program); 120 hours of formal early childhood training, with at least 10 hours in each of the eight CDA subject areas; and 480 hours of work with children ages 3 to 5 within 3 years of applying.
You also build a professional portfolio within 6 months of applying and choose a CDA Professional Development (PD) Specialist. After your application is approved, you take the CDA exam: about 65 questions on a computer at a Pearson VUE test site. Then a PD Specialist does the Verification Visit: reviews your portfolio, watches you work with children and talks with you about your strengths and growth. The Council also offers a faster decision without a visit for some exam results; check its process updates page.
Fees, scholarships and rules change. Check the current amounts on cdacouncil.org, and ask your employer or state about scholarships before you pay. The credential lasts 3 years and is then renewed.
Step by step:
- Choose your setting: Preschool, Infant-Toddler, Family Child Care or Home Visitor.
- Open that setting's page on cdacouncil.org and write down its requirements.
- Find training that covers all eight subject areas.
- Start logging your work hours with children.
- Build your portfolio, apply, take the exam, then have the Verification Visit.
Words to know:
- CDA: Child Development Associate: a national credential for people who work with young children.
- Council for Professional Recognition: the organization that grants the CDA.
- Portfolio: a collection of your own writing and resources that shows your work with children and families.
- Verification Visit: a visit where a PD Specialist watches you work, reviews your portfolio and talks with you.
- PD Specialist: a Professional Development Specialist approved by the Council to do your visit.
Official sources:
- CDA Council: Preschool pathway
- CDA Council: Learn about the CDA
- CDA Council: Process updates
- CDA Council: Find CDA scholarships
- CDA Council: Renew CDA
Try it now: Open the CDA Council page for the setting you want (or use the numbers in this lesson for Preschool). On paper, write the five steps in order and the hours or time window next to each one.
You can now list the steps to the CDA for your setting, with the training hours, work hours and time windows.

check.q: For the Preschool CDA, how is the 120 hours of training spread?
options: All 120 hours in one subject you like
At least 10 hours in each of the eight subject areas
Only hours of work with children
Any 120 hours of online videos
check.why: The Council asks for 120 training hours with no fewer than 10 in each of the eight subject areas.

options: Your state's motor vehicle office
The school your child attends
Any child care center
The Council for Professional Recognition
check.why: The Council for Professional Recognition grants the CDA; a course or employer only helps you prepare.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: A safe and healthy room: licensing, supervision, handwashing, safe sleep
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a child care room for common safety and health problems.
This lesson builds toward: Given a child care room or a description of one, you will check the room for supervision, handwashing, safe sleep and hazard problems, finding at least 4 of 5 planted problems.
Child care is licensed by each state or territory. Licensing sets the minimum health and safety rules a program must meet, such as staff background checks, health and safety training, staff qualifications and inspections. Ratios and training rules differ by state, so look up yours on childcare.gov.
Supervision comes first: you can see and hear every child, you count children often (especially when moving rooms or going outside), and you never leave children alone.
Handwashing stops germs: wash with soap and water, scrubbing for at least 20 seconds, after the bathroom or diapering, before eating or handling food, and after outdoor play. Help children wash too.
Safe sleep for babies: place a baby on their back for every nap and at night, on a firm, flat, level surface with only a fitted sheet. Keep pillows, blankets, bumpers and stuffed toys out of the crib. Also look for hazards: outlets, cords, small objects a young child could choke on, cleaning products within reach, and blocked exits.
Step by step:
- Count the children and check you can see and hear all of them.
- Look for hazards: cords, outlets, small objects, chemicals, blocked exits.
- Check the handwashing area has soap and towels and that adults use it.
- In infant rooms: back to sleep, firm flat surface, nothing in the crib but a fitted sheet.
- Fix what you can now and tell your supervisor about the rest.
Words to know:
- Licensing: the state's minimum health and safety rules a program must meet to operate legally.
- Ratio: how many children one adult may care for; it is set by the state and differs by age.
- Supervision: always being able to see and hear the children in your care.
- Choking hazard: a small object a young child can put in the mouth and choke on.
Official sources:
- Childcare.gov: How is child care regulated?
- Childcare.gov: State and territory resources
- Safe to Sleep (NIH): Safe sleep environment
Try it now: Walk through one room at home (or picture a classroom). List five things you would check for safety and health, and write one fix for each. Then find your state's child care page on childcare.gov and write down who licenses child care there.
You can now check a room for supervision, handwashing, safe sleep and hazard problems, and say who licenses child care in your state.

check.q: A baby falls asleep in a crib. Which setup is safe?
options: On the stomach with a soft blanket
On the side with a pillow for support
On the back, firm mattress, fitted sheet only
On the back with stuffed toys for comfort
check.why: Safe to Sleep says back sleeping on a firm, flat surface with only a fitted sheet.

check.q: Your group comes in from the playground. What do you do first?
options: Count the children
Start the next activity right away
Check your phone
Let them go to the bathroom alone
check.why: Counting at every move makes sure no child was left behind.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Protecting children: mandated reporting
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe the steps to report suspected child abuse or neglect.
This lesson builds toward: Given a story where a child may be harmed, you will describe the steps to report suspected abuse or neglect, calling 911 first if a child is in danger, and following state law and program policy.
In most states, child care workers are mandated reporters. That means the law requires you to report when you have reason to suspect a child is being abused or neglected. You do not need proof. Each state's law says who must report and how, and your program will have a written policy. Learn both before your first day.
If a child is in immediate danger, call 911 first. Otherwise, follow your state's process (often a state child abuse hotline) and your program's policy. If you are unsure where to call, the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline (1-800-422-4453) can help.
Your job is to report, not to investigate. Do not question the child again and again or confront the family. If a child tells you something, stay calm, listen, do not promise to keep it secret, and write down their exact words, the date and the time. Keep it private: share only with the people the law and your policy say.
Step by step:
- If a child is in danger right now, call 911.
- Listen calmly; do not promise to keep a secret.
- Write down what you saw or heard, word for word, with date and time.
- Report as your state law and program policy require.
- Keep it private and do not investigate yourself.
Words to know:
- Mandated reporter: a person the law requires to report suspected child abuse or neglect.
- Neglect: not giving a child the basic care they need, such as food, safety, supervision or medical care.
- Suspect: to have a reason to think something may be happening, without proof.
Official sources:
- Child Welfare Information Gateway: How to report child abuse and neglect
- Childcare.gov: Report a child care concern
Try it now: Look up how to report suspected child abuse in your state (search your state's name plus "report child abuse" and use the .gov page). Write the number or website on a card, with the five steps from this lesson on the back.
You can now describe the steps to report suspected abuse or neglect and find where to report in your state.

check.q: A child tells you a secret about being hurt at home and asks you not to tell. What do you say?
options: "I promise I won't tell anyone."
"Are you sure? Tell me again."
"You must be making that up."
"Thank you for telling me. I need to tell people who can help keep you safe."
check.why: You stay calm and never promise secrecy, because you must report.

check.q: You see marks that worry you, but you have no proof. What does a mandated reporter do?
options: Wait until there is proof
Report as state law and program policy require
Call the parent to ask what happened
Take photos and post them to warn others
check.why: The law asks you to report a reason to suspect; investigating is the agency's job.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Teaching, observing and your CDA plan

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Watching and writing: observation notes
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write an observation note that records only what you saw and heard.
This lesson builds toward: After watching a child play for five minutes, you will write an observation note that records only what you saw and heard, with no labels or guesses, and the date, time and setting included.
Observing and recording children's behavior is one of the eight CDA subject areas. Teachers watch children to learn what each child can do, what they like and what they need next. Good notes also help when you talk with families.
A good note is objective: it says what you saw and heard, not what you think it means. Write "M. stacked six blocks, then knocked them down and laughed" instead of "M. is a happy, smart kid". Labels such as lazy, bad, shy or naughty do not belong in notes.
Include the date, time, setting and the child's first initial. Quote the child's exact words. Keep notes private: they are about a real child and belong to the program.
Step by step:
- Write the date, time, place and the child's first initial.
- Watch for a few minutes.
- Write only actions and exact words.
- Cross out any label or guess.
- Add one question or next step for the child, marked as your idea.
Words to know:
- Observation: watching a child closely to learn what they can do.
- Objective: only facts you can see or hear, with no opinions.
- Anecdotal record: a short written note about one thing a child did or said.
Try it now: Watch a child you know (with the parent's okay), or a children's video, for five minutes. Write an observation note with the date, time and setting. Then circle any word that is a label or guess and rewrite it as a fact.
You can now write a fair, objective observation note with no labels.

check.q: Which sentence belongs in an observation note?
options: "J. is a troublemaker."
"J. seems sad today."
"J. is smarter than the others."
"J. said 'my turn' and took the red truck from T."
check.why: It records only what was seen and heard, with the child's exact words.

check.q: What should every observation note include?
options: Date, time, setting and the child's first initial
The child's full name and home address
Your opinion of the parents
A photo of the child posted online
check.why: Date, time, setting and an initial give context while protecting the child's privacy.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Planning a learning activity
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a short activity plan that fits a child's age.
This lesson builds toward: Given a child's age and interest, you will write a short activity plan with a goal, materials, steps and a safety note, that fits the age and names one CDA subject area.
Young children learn through play. A good activity starts from what children enjoy and can almost do, so it is a small, fun stretch. Advancing children's physical and intellectual development is one of the eight CDA subject areas, and so are social and emotional development and building relationships with families.
A short activity plan has six parts: the age group, a goal (what children will do), the materials, the steps, a safety note, and how you will know it worked. Example for 3- and 4-year-olds: Goal: sort leaves by size. Materials: leaves collected outside, three baskets. Steps: show a big, medium and small leaf; children sort; ask "Which is the biggest?" Safety: wash hands after, check for sharp sticks. How you know: children put most leaves in the right basket and use the words big and small.
Plan for every child: offer an easier and a harder way to do it, use words and pictures, and invite families to send ideas from home. Keep materials large enough that they are not choking hazards for the age.
Step by step:
- Pick the age group and one thing children enjoy.
- Write one goal children will do.
- List safe, free or low-cost materials.
- Write 3 to 5 steps.
- Add a safety note and how you will know it worked.
- Name the CDA subject area it supports.
Words to know:
- Developmentally appropriate: fits what children of that age can usually do, with a small stretch.
- Fine motor: small movements of the hands and fingers, like picking up or cutting.
- Gross motor: big movements of the body, like running, jumping or climbing.
Try it now: Write a one-page activity plan for children ages 3 to 5 using things you have at home (cups, socks, paper, leaves). Include all six parts and name the CDA subject area it supports.
You can now write a short, safe activity plan that fits the children's age and names a CDA subject area.

options: Write a full paragraph about leaves
Sort leaves into big and small
Do long division with leaves
Read a science textbook alone
check.why: Sorting by size is a small, playful stretch for preschool children.

check.q: Your plan for 3-year-olds uses small beads. What is missing from the plan?
options: A longer list of steps
A harder goal
A safety note: beads are a choking hazard, so use larger items
More beads
check.why: Every plan needs a safety note, and small items are a choking risk for young children.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your portfolio, the exam, the visit and your plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Make a dated CDA preparation plan from training to Verification Visit.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own calendar, you will make a dated CDA preparation plan from training to Verification Visit, that keeps experience within 3 years and the portfolio within 6 months of applying.
The portfolio holds your own writing and resources about your work with children and families. The Council's Competency Standards book for your setting (for Preschool, the green edition) explains exactly what goes in it. Get the book early and fill the portfolio as you go; it must be finished within 6 months of applying.
Plan backwards from the dates that matter. Work hours count only if they are within 3 years of your application, so start a simple log now: date, place, ages and hours, signed by a supervisor if your program allows. Pick training that covers all eight subject areas and keep every certificate.
Prepare for the exam by reviewing the eight subject areas, practicing scenario questions like the ones in this course, and booking a Pearson VUE test site after you get your Ready to Schedule notice. Before the Verification Visit, practice talking about your strengths and one area you are growing in. Check every fee and step on cdacouncil.org, and ask about scholarships.
Step by step:
- Write today's date and your setting.
- Pick a training program and a target date to finish the 120 hours.
- Start a work-hours log and set a date to reach the hours your setting needs.
- Set a portfolio start date and an apply date within 6 months of it.
- Add target months for the exam and the Verification Visit.
- Put the dates in your phone calendar or on a paper calendar.
Words to know:
- Competency Standards book: the Council's book for your setting that explains the portfolio and standards.
- Ready to Schedule notice: the Council's message that you may now book your exam or visit.
- Work-hours log: a record of the dates and hours you worked with children.
Official sources:
- CDA Council: Preschool pathway
- CDA Council: Educator pathways (all settings)
- Pearson VUE: CDA exam
Try it now: Final task: make your CDA preparation plan with real dates for training, work hours, portfolio, applying, the exam and the Verification Visit. Attach your activity plan from Lesson 5 as your first portfolio-style piece.
You can now turn the CDA steps into your own plan with dates, ready to start.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Requirements right Steps are missing or the hours and time windows are wrong. Lists the setting, 120 training hours across all eight subject areas, the work hours, portfolio, exam and visit correctly. Also notes the current fee, a scholarship to apply for and the renewal date, all checked on cdacouncil.org. Dated plan No dates, or dates that break the 3-year or 6-month windows. Real target dates for each step that keep experience within 3 years and the portfolio within 6 months of applying. Includes a work-hours log started today and calendar reminders. Activity plan Missing a goal, safety note or way to check it worked. Age, goal, materials, steps, safety note, how you will know it worked and a CDA subject area. Adds an easier and harder version and one way to involve families. Safety thinking The activity or plan ignores supervision, handwashing or choking hazards. The safety note covers supervision and any hazard in the materials. Names who licenses child care in their state and one training it requires. Observation and reporting ready Sample note uses labels, or no state reporting contact is written down. Includes one objective observation note and the state's reporting contact card. The note leads to a clear next step for the child, marked as the learner's idea. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check it again.

check.q: You worked in a preschool four years ago and want to apply next month. What should you check?
options: Nothing; all past hours count forever
Whether you still need a diploma
Whether the exam is optional
Whether your hours fall within 3 years of your application
check.why: Experience hours must be within 3 years of submitting your application.

check.q: When should you start your work-hours log?
options: Now, from your first day with children
After you pass the exam
Only after the Verification Visit
Never; the Council counts them for you
check.why: A log from day one keeps your hours and dates clear when you apply.
